subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Stellar-Mass Black Holes
description: A fast breakdown of Stellar-Mass Black Holes for builders.

hook.text: Stellar-mass black holes weigh 5 to 100 times the Sun's mass. They're the most common type we know about.

buildup.text: They form when massive stars die. The Milky Way alone may contain 100 million of them.

discovery.text: Cygnus X-1, discovered in the 1960s, was the first strong black hole candidate. It pulls gas from a companion star.

twist.text: Most stellar black holes are invisible and solitary. We find them only when they interact with nearby matter.

climax.text: Gaia BH1, found in 2022, is the closest known black hole—just 1,560 light-years away, quietly orbiting a Sun-like star.

punchline.text: A hundred million in our galaxy alone. Most are completely invisible.

quiz.question: How many stellar-mass black holes might exist in the Milky Way?

details.summary: Stellar-mass black holes, typically 5-100 times the Sun's mass, are the most common type. Born from collapsed massive stars, they're detected when they orbit companion stars and pull matter into superheated accretion disks that emit X-rays, or through gravitational waves when they merge.
details.whyItMatters: Stellar-mass black holes are the most abundant and most directly observable type. They were the first confirmed through X-ray observations and the first detected via gravitational waves.
takeaways: They range from about 5 to 100 solar masses
Born from the collapse of massive stars
Detected via X-ray binaries and gravitational waves

faq.question: How many stellar-mass black holes exist in our galaxy?
faq.answer: Estimates suggest 100 million to a billion in the Milky Way alone. Most are isolated and invisible, detected only when they interact with nearby matter or another compact object. Only a few dozen have been confirmed observationally through X-ray or gravitational wave detections.

faq.question: What is the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes?
faq.answer: For years, no compact objects were found between about 2.5 and 5 solar masses, suggesting a gap. Recent gravitational wave detections have found objects in this range, challenging the clear division. Whether this gap is real or observational remains an active research question.
